messages.subject: Appropriateness of gdistsamp
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked community,

My goal is to model variation in Bornean orangutan densities in response to changes in fruit availability over time. I would very much appreciate feedback on the appropriateness of using gdistsamp for this.

The research question is to what extent do orangutans track changes in food availability across the landscape. The data consist of distance sampling and phenology measurements at 12 sites along an elevational gradient collected over 64 months.

The environment is aseasonal, meaning there are no particular times of year in which fruit is more readily available. Instead, fruit availability is characterized by boom and bust cycles that occur over multiple years and are believed to be triggered by ENSO events. In addition, orangutans are very long-lived and have extremely slow life histories with adult females reproducing on average once every 6-8 years. Births and deaths during this 64-month period were therefore likely quite low.

My questions are:

1) Would it be appropriate to set up the observation covariate matrix of M sites x T years as the 12 sites by 64 months?

2) If so, should I build temporal dependence between months as an availability covariate?

3) If sites are not fully spatially independent, how much might this affect the density estimates?

Thank you very much,
Lydia

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Appropriateness of gdistsamp
messages.body_plain:
hi Lydia,
 I think the gdistsamp models are appropriate for your situation.

 (1) yes

 (2) I think thats reasonable. Alternatively you could stack the replicate samples on top of each other and treat them as new "sites". If the animals are mixing over the landscape in response to food availability then the effective site (scale at which relevant covariates are measured) seems to me to be a "site x time" . The within site dynamics maybe aren't that important.

 (3) depends on how non-independent they are. I assume you mean that some individuals can show up in > 1 transect?  The effect of this non-independence is, I think, to produce some bias in standard errors which I'm guessing is really negligible if the overlap is not too great. The only way to address this explicitly is with simulation I think.

regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andy,

Thanks so much, this is very helpful. I think that your suggestion to stack the months might help clarify another question I have, which is the appropriate interpretation of the lambda and phi parameters from the following model:

mHC.1 <- gdistsamp(~ elevation, ~ No.stemsfruit, ~ replicates, data=OHunmarkedGDS, output="density", unitsOut="kmsq", mixture="NB", keyfun="hazard", K=500)

At this point I have been interpreting lambda as the density of orangutans “belonging to a site” and phi as the probability than an orangutan that belongs to a site is present in that site given the number of stems with fruit. Sine we believe that the animals move fairly freely about the landscape in response to food, would stacking the months allow us move us away from this interpretation and instead allow us to estimate densities without the constraint of the animals “belonging to a site”?

In terms of the spatial non-independence, yes, exactly the animals might show up in more than one site during a month because they were monitored on different days and the animals can reach all of sites within a few days.

Thanks again,
Lydia

messages.body_plain:
hi Lydia,
 I agree, the interpretation of phi is problematic because individuals are moving freely over the landscape. So the notion of "belonging to a site" is kind of nonsense.
 Stacking the data is therefore probably a better approach.
 Even with the dependence induced by individuals being at multiple sites, I think the inferences will be valid about "site x time" covariates such as local food availability.

I would recommend doing a simulation study where you evaluate the validity of inferences by a simulation study.

regards
andy

messages.subject: Habitat-specific density estimates (birds)
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone

Sorry to have to post to the list, I was hoping to find an answer on a discussion or in one of the R vignettes, but couldn't. I have something of a problem because my analysis plans have changed since I collected data, meaning my study design is less than optimal!

I have a study consisting of:
25 1 km^2 squares ("sites") in variably heterogenous habitats. i.e. some are uniform forest/pasture, others are mixes of two or more habitat types.
Within each site I have 12 "points", visited once each, where I conducted point counts with distance sampling for birds.
At each point I know the coverage of different habitats, again this is variably heterogenous.
Using the count data for each bird species at each point and the variable proportions of different habitats at each point, I would like to estimate the mean density in each habitat type (eventually for each species, but one to begin with would be a start!).
My plan was to use a modified version of the models used by Royle et al. 2004, with proportion of each habitat type as a covariate within the Poisson model (presumably arcsin transformed?!) and site as a random effect in the model.

However... a) I wasn't sure whether this was actually a good idea b) I couldn't find details of the specific functions Royle et al. used c) a later paper (Sillett et al.  2012) explicitly states that their update of Royle et al.'s model "assumes that density is constant within each plot", which is the opposite of what I want to assume. Is it possible to get around this?

Sorry the verbosity and vagueness, any help or pointers would be gratefully received.

David

Royle, J. A., Dawson, D. K., & Bates, S. (2004). MODELING ABUNDANCE EFFECTS IN DISTANCE SAMPLING. Ecology, 85(6), 1591–1597. doi:10.1890/03-3127

Sillett, T. S., CHANDLER, R. B., Royle, J. A., KÉRY, M., & Morrison, S. A. (2012). Hierarchical distance-sampling models to estimate population size and habitat-specific abundance of an island endemic. Ecological Applications, 22(7), 1997–2006.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Habitat-specific density estimates (birds)
messages.body_plain:
hi David,

 unmarked will not handle random effects. For this, I suggest using WinBUGS (see the Kery 2010 and Kery and Schaub 2011 books for many examples and templates, although not about distance sampling).

 If you don't pursue the random effects then I agree you could use "% habitat type x" as a set of covariates in the mean:
 log(lambda(point)) = beta0 + beta1*log(x1) + beta2*log(x2) + ....
 which I think is pretty standard for modeling compositional data. Or maybe using some other transformation as you suggest.

 Ideally you would parameterize the Poisson mean like this:

 lambda(point) = sum_{k} lambda(k)*xk

where the xk sum to 1.  That is, express the expected density as an area-weighted sum of the constituent pieces. This would be easy to do in WinBUGS but not in unmarked.

regards
andy

Hi all,

I am running open occ models like the following:  (fm30<- colext(~1, ~1, ~scale(warea), ~1, occ.umf))

Notice I am scaling the continuous covariate(warea) within the formula.  I saw in Richard's reply to a previous thread  (Model predictions when scaling covariates , from March 2011)  that when you use "predict" after a model such as this, the backtransformation/rescaling is already performed.  warea.ext<-backTransform(linearComb(fm30,type="ext",coefficients=c(0,1)))
> warea.ext
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Extinction estimate(s)

 Estimate     SE LinComb (Intercept) scale(warea)
   0.0039 0.0134   -5.54           0            1

However, when compared to output from the model summary I noticed that while the parameter estimates are the same, the standard error estimates here do NOT correspond with the  backtransformed estimates I get from that output (see below).  The SEs are very different-- which method is correct (if either??).

Extinction (logit-scale):
             Estimate   SE     z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)     -4.32 2.33 -1.85  0.0639
scale(warea)    -5.54 3.46 -1.60  0.1092

[1] 0.00391117    #same parameter estimate as above
> plogis(3.46)
[1] 0.969528       #DIFFERENT SE estimate from above

Thanks for any help with this!
Tamara Pandolfo

hi Tamara,
 The reason for this is because the variance of a function of a parameter is not simply the function of the variance UNLESS the function is linear.  In the present case, the function is the inverse-logit function and unmarked uses a delta approximation to compute the variance.
 if x is your random variable with var(x)  and your transformation is:

 y = exp(x)/(1+exp(x))

 then the delta approximation yields:

 var(y) = (exp(x)/[  (1+exp(x) )^2 ])^2   * var(x)

 so, in the example you provided, the SE is the square-root of the expression above:

> exp(-5.54)/((1+exp(-5.54))^2) * 3.46
[1] 0.01347972
>

regards
andy

messages.subject: Which Fitting Function to Pick?
messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked users group,

I am a PhD student at Emory University, new to using unmarked, and will appreciate any suggestions or advice you can share. I hope this question is appropriate for this group.

I have a large avian point count dataset.  Eight sites were counted by two observers once per month (June-October) for two years, using 10-minute unlimited radius point counts, which recorded all avian species detected during the count.  The primary observer recorded distances in his count, while the secondary observer did not.  Furthermore, the primary observer was present for all counts while the secondary observer was present at about 75% of the counts.

I am interested in obtaining the abundance of various species at each site.  After reading the documentation about unmarked, I understand that I will need to make a separate model for each species of interest as there does not appear to be a way to model the abundances of multiple species at once (but please correct me if I am mistaken).

What I hope you can help me with is deciding which fitting function in unmarked to pick that will yield the must robust abundance estimates, given that my data seem able to fit under several of the fitting functions, as I have: repeated counts (pcount), multiple season counts (pcountopen), distance sampling in the case of one observer (distsamp), and dual observer counts (multnompois, gmultmix).  Because I need to make abundance estimates for up to 30 different species in each site, it is not feasible for me to fit models for each species using each of the possible functions and then compare the estimates.  Instead, I am hoping that someone can help me decide which function, given the many that it seems I can use with my data, will be most appropriate to make the most robust estimates of species abundance at each site.

Many thanks for any help you can provide,
Rebecca

messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

I have now analyzed the stacked orangutan data and have follow-up questions about error messages and estimates that seem too high.

An initial comparison of null models showed that the negative binomial distribution produced lower AIC values. I ran 10 models of interest using the NB distribution.

The default optim method produced the error message “Hessian is singular. Try using fewer covariates and supplying starting values” despite either using zero covariates. When I provided starting values, the error message “Error in optim(starts, nll, method = method, hessian = se, ...) : initial value in 'vmmin' is not finite” occurred. I was only able to get NB models (with 0-3 lambda covariates) to run by setting optim=SANN. The lambda estimates from the best-fit model were high (min: 2.6, median: 3.7, max: 49.2 orangutans/kmsq). Previous density estimates of orangutans at this site using the program DISTANCE range from a minimum of 0.5 to a maximum of 3.5 orangutans/kmsq.

Following the guidance of other forum posts, I then re-ran the 10 models using the Poisson distribution and the default optim method in the hopes that estimates would decrease, but instead they were extremely inflated (e.g. 200 orangutans/km sq).

My questions are:

1)    Might SANN be contributing to inflated estimates? If so, do you have any suggestions for dealing with the error terms caused by other optimization methods?

2)    What else might be causing estimates to be so high? It is possible that these animals are just too few and far between on the ground for the models to work well predicting their occurrence?

Thank you very much in advance,

Lydia

messages.body_plain:
Hello all;

I am modeling lizard abundance in 1260 sq m patches across a small island. Each of 41 sites was sampled 6 times (double independent observers). I am using each observer's survey as a site visit, and we collected 12 site (environmental) and 1 survey (observer) covariate. After using the dredge function on models for abundance (~1 ~..covariates..) or detection (~.covariates.. ~1), I used the top abundance and detection covariates in a model. The model doesn't improved when I add or delete covariates on either side. I used parboot with 100 simulations and GOF was fine. The model is here:

> mAbunD

Call:
pcount(formula = ~Distance.from.Enclosure + Cover.Percent + Habitat +
    AvgT.OTM + MaxT.Hobo + MaxT.OTM ~ Distance.from.Enclosure +
    LLDepth + Woody.stems + AvgT.Hobo + AvgT.OTM, data = buckRM)

Abundance:
                                        Estimate       SE      z     P(>|z|)
(Intercept)                         4.37476 2.549431   1.72   8.62e-02
Distance.from.Enclosure   -0.00473 0.000373 -12.67   8.44e-37
LLDepth                          -0.19061 0.041985  -4.54    5.63e-06
Woody.stems                 -0.05090 0.016867  -3.02     2.55e-03
AvgT.Hobo                     -0.24658 0.102684  -2.40    1.63e-02
AvgT.OTM                       0.26193 0.087816   2.98    2.86e-03

Detection:
                                           Estimate       SE     z     P(>|z|)
(Intercept)                          3.969698 2.172067  1.83   0.067608
Distance.from.Enclosure   -0.000982 0.000283 -3.48    0.000511
Cover.Percent                      -0.009896 0.002592 -3.82 0.000135
Habitat2                            0.250099 0.113097  2.21    0.027011
Habitat3                          -0.279203 0.099127 -2.82    0.004853
AvgT.OTM                         -0.270873 0.089419 -3.03   0.002452
MaxT.Hobo                        0.021481 0.005779  3.72   0.000201
MaxT.OTM                         0.037335 0.010725  3.48  0.000499

AIC: 910.0409

Then, I found site abundance using:

>abund<-ranef(mAbunD, K=500)
>EBUP<-bup(abund,stat="mode")
> sum(bup(abund))  ##get abundance estimate
>CI<-confint(abund, level=0.9)
> colSums(CI)

I am plotting curves of the individual covariates using this sort of code:
>newData2 <- data.frame(AvgT.OTM=seq(25,50,by=0.5), Cover.Percent=0, Distance.from.Enclosure=0,Habitat=factor(2,levels=c(1,2,3)), MaxT.Hobo=0,MaxT.OTM=0)

Richard can jump in here and correct me if I'm wrong, but I think I know the answer to this one:

First off, when you use dynamics="trend" in pcountOpen you omit the omega parameter and the trend (actually the finite rate of population increase) is represented by gamma.

Then, yes, the last value of the yearly site covs is ignored for the analysis, just like in the default parameterization. You can convince yourself of this by putting NA for the last value and you will see you get the same result.

Finally, I think your two equations for N[i,t] are both slightly off.  It might be better represented by this:

N[i,t] ~ Poisson(lambda)
N[i,t+1] ~ Poisson(N[i,t] gamma)

It gets complicated when thinking about how to model it or present the results because the finite rate of increase (gamma) which is our estimate of trend is calculated for the interval between two sampling periods. Thus, when you have yearly site covs, there will be one less value for gamma than for the N's.

messages.body_plain:
In my way of thinking, the gamma covariates aren't taken from year t or year t-1. The covariates for a gamma parameter in year t are taken from the interval from year t-1 to year t. If you have 10 years of survey data you will have 10 estimates of abundance, but only 9 estimates of the finite rate of increase (usually called lambda, but called gamma here since lambda is used already). Thus, for each covariate on gamma (i.e yearly site covariate) you will need 9 columns of actual data and a 10th column that is not used. There is a one-to-one correspondence between the gamma values and the gamma covariates.

If you have a covariate for the "trend" in the population that is only measured each year at the same time you do your survey, then you will have to decide whether you think the value from t-1 or from t will best explain the trend in the population. In the anlaysis I am working on we have a value that is measured during the interval between surveys that we think should affect the trend in the population.

Dear Cristina,

I would say that the huge SEs are a sign of either non-convergence, or more likely, of non-identifiability of the parameters for your data set. In principle, all such parameters should be identifiable, and in particular, it should not be a problem when you have the same covariates on different ones of the 4 logistic regressions that represents the dynocc model. However, with finite sample sizes you may well run into trouble.

The other question about the R2: This is non-trivial in a mixed model such as this one. I would say that with unmarked, you can't compute any R2-alike. In a Bayesian approach you could treat site- and/or year-effects as random and as coming from a normal distribution with a variance to be estimated (and no covariates). Then, you would fit the same model with some covariates. The proportional reduction in the site- or the year random effects variance could be interpreted as the proportion of the variance that is explained by that covariate(s). However, this is something that would have to be computed for each of the four logistic regressions separately.

Kind regards --  Marc
